subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Benign breast disease and inflammatory processes
vignette: A 38-year-old woman presents with bilateral breast pain and multiple lumps that vary with her menstrual cycle, worsening premenstrually. Examination shows diffuse, mobile, bilateral nodularity.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition and its cancer risk?

options.text: A single, well-defined mobile fibroglandular tumor with no increased cancer risk
Dilation of subareolar ducts with inflammation and fibrosis in a smoker
Nonproliferative fibrocystic changes (simple cysts, apocrine metaplasia, stromal fibrosis) with no increased cancer risk
Proliferative sclerosing adenosis with calcifications and a slight increased risk
Blood-filled ovarian cysts from ectopic endometrium

explanation_correct: Fibrocystic changes are the most common benign breast condition in premenopausal women aged 20-50, presenting with premenstrual breast pain and lumps that are often bilateral and multifocal. Nonproliferative lesions include simple cysts (fluid-filled duct dilation, 'blue dome'), papillary apocrine metaplasia, and stromal fibrosis; these do not increase cancer risk. Proliferative forms (sclerosing adenosis, epithelial hyperplasia) carry increased risk.

explanation_incorrect.A: A small, well-defined mobile fibroglandular mass describes a fibroadenoma, not the diffuse bilateral cycle-related nodularity of fibrocystic change.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dilation of subareolar ducts with inflammation and fibrosis in a smoker describes mammary duct ectasia, which presents with multicolored discharge and an inverted nipple.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sclerosing adenosis is a proliferative fibrocystic change with calcifications and a slight increased cancer risk, not the nonproliferative, no-risk form described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Blood-filled cysts from ectopic endometrium are endometriomas of the ovary, unrelated to breast fibrocystic change.

educationalObjective: Nonproliferative fibrocystic changes (simple cysts, apocrine metaplasia, stromal fibrosis) are common in premenopausal women and do not increase cancer risk.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Benign breast disease and inflammatory processes
vignette: A breast biopsy in a 45-year-old woman shows increased numbers of acini with stromal fibrosis and associated calcifications. Another area shows increased cells in the terminal duct lobular epithelium, some with atypical features. The pathologist notes these proliferative changes affect future cancer risk.
question: Which of the following best states the cancer risk associated with these proliferative fibrocystic changes?

options.text: Sclerosing adenosis slightly increases risk; epithelial hyperplasia with atypical cells increases risk of carcinoma
Both lesions confer no increased risk, as with simple cysts
Both lesions are obligate precancers that will inevitably progress to invasive cancer
Only stromal fibrosis increases risk, via malignant transformation of fibroblasts
The risk is identical to that of a simple cyst or apocrine metaplasia

explanation_correct: Proliferative fibrocystic lesions carry an increased risk of breast cancer. Sclerosing adenosis (acini with stromal fibrosis and associated calcifications) confers a slight increase in risk. Epithelial hyperplasia (increased cells in terminal ductal or lobular epithelium) increases the risk of carcinoma, particularly when atypical cells are present. This contrasts with nonproliferative lesions such as simple cysts, apocrine metaplasia, and stromal fibrosis, which do not raise risk.

explanation_incorrect.B: Simple cysts and other nonproliferative lesions do not raise risk, but proliferative lesions like sclerosing adenosis and atypical hyperplasia do.
explanation_incorrect.C: Proliferative lesions increase risk but are not obligate precancers that inevitably progress to invasive carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: Stromal fibrosis is a nonproliferative change and does not transform into malignancy; the risk relates to the epithelial proliferation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Proliferative lesions carry a higher risk than simple cysts or apocrine metaplasia, which are nonproliferative and not associated with increased risk.

educationalObjective: Sclerosing adenosis slightly increases breast cancer risk, and epithelial hyperplasia with atypical cells increases it further, unlike nonproliferative fibrocystic changes.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Benign breast disease and inflammatory processes
vignette: A 50-year-old woman has a painless breast lump. Mammography shows a calcified oil cyst. She does not recall any specific injury. Biopsy shows necrotic fat cells and multinucleated giant cells.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Lactational mastitis
Mammary duct ectasia
Invasive ductal carcinoma
Fat necrosis
Fibroadenoma

explanation_correct: Fat necrosis is a benign, usually painless breast lump that results from injury to breast tissue. Mammography can show a calcified oil cyst, and biopsy shows necrotic fat with multinucleated giant cells. Importantly, up to 50% of patients do not report any trauma, so a lack of reported injury does not exclude it.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lactational mastitis occurs during breastfeeding, presents with pain, warmth, and erythema from bacterial infection (usually S. aureus), and would not show a calcified oil cyst with necrotic fat and giant cells.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mammary duct ectasia is dilation of subareolar ducts with inflammation and fibrosis, associated with smoking and presenting with multicolored discharge and an inverted nipple, not a calcified oil cyst.
explanation_incorrect.C: Invasive ductal carcinoma is a malignant rock-hard mass with small glandular cells in desmoplastic stroma, not necrotic fat and giant cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibroadenoma is a small, mobile, well-defined fibrous and glandular tumor in younger women, not a calcified oil cyst with giant cells.

educationalObjective: Fat necrosis is a benign painless lump with a calcified oil cyst and necrotic fat/giant cells; many patients report no trauma.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Benign breast disease and inflammatory processes
vignette: A 28-year-old woman who is breastfeeding a 3-week-old infant develops a painful, warm, erythematous area of the breast with fever. She has a cracked nipple.
question: Which of the following is the most likely causative organism and the appropriate management?

options.text: Escherichia coli; discontinue breastfeeding and start antibiotics
Staphylococcus aureus; treat with antibiotics and continue breastfeeding
Candida albicans; treat with topical antifungals only
Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus); antibiotics and stop breastfeeding
Mycobacterium tuberculosis; multi-drug antitubercular therapy

explanation_correct: Lactational mastitis occurs during breastfeeding, with increased risk of bacterial infection through cracks in the nipple. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen. Treatment is with antibiotics, and patients should continue breastfeeding, which helps resolve the infection and prevents milk stasis.

explanation_incorrect.A: E. coli is not the most common cause of lactational mastitis, and breastfeeding should generally be continued rather than discontinued.
explanation_incorrect.C: Candida can cause nipple thrush, but it is not the typical bacterial cause of lactational mastitis described with a cracked nipple and fever.
explanation_incorrect.D: Group B Streptococcus is associated with neonatal sepsis, not the common cause of lactational mastitis; breastfeeding need not be stopped.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tuberculous mastitis is rare and not the typical acute breastfeeding-associated infection; it would not present this way.

educationalObjective: Lactational mastitis is usually caused by S. aureus entering through nipple cracks; treat with antibiotics and continue breastfeeding.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Benign breast disease and inflammatory processes
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with a long smoking history presents with areolar pain, a multicolored nipple discharge, and an inverted nipple. Examination shows a periareolar mass.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: A small fibroepithelial tumor within a lactiferous duct beneath the areola
A benign, mobile, well-circumscribed fibroglandular mass in a woman under 35
Nonproliferative fibrocystic change with blue-dome cysts
Dermal lymphatic invasion by carcinoma causing peau d'orange
Dilation of subareolar ducts with inflammation and fibrosis (mammary duct ectasia)

explanation_correct: Mammary duct ectasia is dilation of the subareolar ducts with inflammation and fibrosis. It is associated with smoking and presents with areolar pain, multicolored (often greenish or brownish) nipple discharge, an inverted nipple, and a periareolar mass. It is a benign inflammatory process.

explanation_incorrect.A: Intraductal papilloma is a small fibroepithelial tumor within a lactiferous duct beneath the areola and is the most common cause of unilateral serous or bloody nipple discharge, not multicolored discharge with duct ectasia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fibroadenoma is a small, mobile, well-defined fibroglandular mass typically in women under 35, not an areolar inflammatory process with discharge and inversion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Fibrocystic change with blue-dome cysts produces cyclical bilateral pain and lumps, not a periareolar mass with an inverted nipple and multicolored discharge.
explanation_incorrect.D: Inflammatory carcinoma involves dermal lymphatic invasion with warm, swollen, erythematous peau d'orange skin and a poor prognosis, not the chronic multicolored discharge of duct ectasia.

educationalObjective: Mammary duct ectasia is a benign, smoking-associated dilation of subareolar ducts causing areolar pain, multicolored discharge, nipple inversion, and a periareolar mass.
